 Jury finds Manassas Park man Naresh Bhatt guilty of murdering, dismembering wife
 By Alan Etter 
 November 10, 2026 | 
 3:56 PM 
 | 
 A jury in Prince William County, Virginia, has convicted Naresh Bhatt of first-degree murder in the 2024 killing of his wife, Mamta Kafle Bhatt.
 Naresh Bhatt was also found guilty of two other felony charges: concealing a dead body and defiling a dead body. He’s scheduled for sentencing March 12.
 Closing statements concluded Tuesday in the murder trial of Naresh Bhatt, and the jury returned its verdict the same day. In stunning testimony last week , the Manassas Park man said he discovered his wife dead in their home. He said it appeared she took poison. But then he said he panicked and, out of fear of being blamed for her death, decided to dismember and then dispose of his wife’s corpse. Naresh Bhatt insisted he did not kill his wife.
 Her body has still not been found.
 Just before the jury got the case, Assistant Commonwealth’s Attorney Katherine Williams said none of that explanation makes any sense.
 “Even though he cut up Mamta’s body, even though he stuffed her in the garbage can, he had nothing to do with her death? Come on, that is ridiculous,” Williams said to the jury. “The defendant murdered Mamta Kafle, dismembered Mamta Kafle and the defendant got rid of her like garbage,” she said.
 In her final statement to the jury, defense counsel Tracey Lenox said that if there was even the slightest doubt — they must acquit Naresh Bhatt of murder.
 “The possibility, indeed even the probability of guilt in the American system of government must be met not with a guilty verdict,” Lenox said.
 Jurors spent the morning hearing from additional witnesses saying the Bhatts had a terrible marriage, with one witness describing physical abuse of Mamta Kafle Bhatt.
 Through tears, Mamta’s colleague and close friend Sunita Basnet Thapa said she knew the Bhatts’ marriage was failing and that Mamta told her she was emotionally abused by Naresh Bhatt.
 “She was tortured for a long time, and she was still tortured,” Basnet Thapa said. When asked by prosecutor Williams if her friend told her about any physical abuse, Basnet Thapa cried, “Yes, she did.”
 A psychologist testified that Naresh Bhatt meets the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder, explaining that when he was in the military he was sexually assaulted by Maoist rebels who captured and detained him in Nepal.

 Appeals court limits order for LinkedIn to disclose journalists’ communications in leak probe
 By The Associated Press 
 November 10, 2026 | 
 4:56 PM 
 | 
 WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge must narrow an order requiring LinkedIn to divulge journalists' communications on the social media platform to the Trump administration as part of a leak investigation, a federal appeals court ruled Tuesday in a case with profound free-speech implications.
A three-judge panel from the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the government isn't entitled to a “blanket” order for LinkedIn to disclose a broad array of user records belonging to the journalists, whose employer isn't identified in court records.
“A request by the government to scoop up reporters’ records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health,” Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III wrote in the court's unanimous opinion.
But the panel also rejected LinkedIn's request to entirely quash the district court's "substantially overbroad” disclosure order. The panel recognized that the journalists' First Amendment rights must be balanced against the administration's duty to protect national security information.
